entries.567fd22734f6d6ec3b1ecf827d2c6b49d22cb009: <div sID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Neh.4" sID="Neh.4"/> <div eID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8775" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> We left all hands at work for the building of the wall about Jerusalem. But such good work is not wont to be carried on without opposition; now here we are told what opposition was given to it, and what methods Nehemiah took to forward the work, notwithstanding that opposition. I. Their enemies reproached and ridiculed their undertaking, but their scoffs they answered with prayers: they heeded them not, but went on with their work notwithstanding, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.1-Neh.2.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. They formed a bloody design against them, to hinder them by force of arms, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.7-Neh.2.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.10-Neh.2.12">10-12</reference>. To guard against this Nehemiah prayed (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.9">ver. 9</reference>), set guards (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.13">ver. 13</reference>), and encouraged them to fight (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.14">ver. 14</reference>), by which the design was broken (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.15">ver. 15</reference>), and so the work was carried on with all needful precaution against a surprise, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.16-Neh.2.23">ver. 16-23</reference>. In all this Nehemiah approved himself a man of great wisdom and courage, as well as great piety.
entries.194f0636b505cad10a4ce88158b06a9d7f1abc57: <div eID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8775" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Opposition of Sanballat, &c.. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 445.)</title> <div sID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But it came to pass, that when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned? <hi type="super">3</hi> Now Tobiah the Ammonite <hi type="italic">was</hi> by him, and he said, Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall. <hi type="super">4</hi> Hear, O our God; for we are despised: and turn their reproach upon their own head, and give them for a prey in the land of captivity: <hi type="super">5</hi> And cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee: for they have provoked <hi type="italic">thee</hi> to anger before the builders. <hi type="super">6</hi> So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work. <div eID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The spiteful scornful reflection which Sanballat and Tobiah cast upon the Jews for their attempt to build the wall about Jerusalem. The country rang of it presently; intelligence was brought of it to Samaria, that nest of enemies to the Jews and their prosperity; and here we are told how they received the tidings. 1. In heart. They were very angry at the undertaking, and had <hi type="italic">great indignation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.4.1">v. 1</reference>. It vexed them that Nehemiah came to seek the welfare of the children of Israel (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>); but, when they heard of this great undertaking for their good, they were out of all patience. They had hitherto pleased themselves with the thought that while Jerusalem was unwalled they could swallow it up and make themselves masters of it when they pleased; but, if it be walled, it will not only be fenced against them, but by degrees become formidable to them. The strength and safety of the church are the grief and vexation of its enemies. 2. In word. They despised it, and made it the subject of their ridicule. In this they sufficiently displayed their malice; but good was brought out of it; for, looking upon it as a foolish undertaking that would sink under its own weight, they did not go about to obstruct it till it was too late. Let us see with what pride and malice they set themselves publicly to banter it. (1.) Sanballat speaks with scorn of the workmen: "<hi type="italic">These feeble Jews</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.2">v. 2</reference>), "what will they do for materials? <hi type="italic">Will they revive the stones out of the rubbish?</hi> And what mean they by being so hasty? Do they think to make the walling of a city but one day's work, and to keep the feast of dedication with sacrifice the next day? Poor silly people! See how ridiculous they make themselves!" (2.) Tobiah speaks with no less scorn of the work itself. He has his jest too, and must show his wit, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.3">v. 3</reference>. Profane scoffers sharpen one another. "Sorry work," says he, "they are likely to make of it; they themselves will be ashamed of it: <hi type="italic">If a fox go up,</hi> not with his subtlety, but with his weight, he <hi type="italic">will break down their stone wall.</hi>" Many a good work has been thus looked upon with contempt by the <hi type="italic">proud and haughty scorners.</hi> <div eID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> II. Nehemiah's humble and devout address to God when he heard of these reflections. He had notice brought him of what they said. It is probable that they themselves sent him a message to this purport, to discourage him, hoping to jeer him out of his attempt; but he did not answer these fools according to their folly; he did not upbraid them with their weakness, but looked up to God by prayer. <div eID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> 1. He begs of God to take notice of the indignities that were done them (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.4">v. 4</reference>), and in this we are to imitate him: <hi type="italic">Hear, O our God! for we are despised.</hi> Note, (1.) God's people have often been a despised people, and loaded with contempt. (2.) God does, and will, hear all the slights that are put upon his people, and it is their comfort that he does so and a good reason why they should be as though they were deaf, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">15</reference>. "Thou art our God to whom we appeal; our cause needs no more than a fair hearing." <div eID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> 2. He begs of God to avenge their cause and turn the reproach upon the enemies themselves (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.4-Neh.4.5">v. 4, 5</reference>); and this was spoken rather by a spirit of prophecy than by a spirit of prayer, and is not to be imitated by us who are taught of Christ to <hi type="italic">pray for</hi> those that <hi type="italic">despitefully use and persecute us.</hi> Christ himself prayed for those that reproached him: <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them.</hi> Nehemiah here prays, <hi type="italic">Cover not their iniquity.</hi> Note, (1.) Those that cast contempt on God's people do but prepare everlasting shame for themselves. (2.) It is a sin from which sinners are seldom recovered. Doubtless Nehemiah had reason to think the hearts of those sinners were desperately hardened, so that they would never repent of it, else he would not have prayed that it might <hi type="italic">never be blotted out.</hi> The reason he gives is not, <hi type="italic">They have abused us,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">They have provoked thee,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">before the builders,</hi> to whom, it is likely, they sent a spiteful message. Note, We should be angry at the malice of persecutors, not because it is abusive to us, but because it is offensive to God; and on that we may ground an expectation that God will appear against it, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">Ps. lxxiv. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">22</reference>. <div eID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> III. The vigour of the builders, notwithstanding these reflections, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.6">v. 6</reference>. They made such good speed that in a little time they had run up the wall to half its height, for <hi type="italic">the people had a mind to work;</hi> their hearts were upon it, and they would have it forwarded. Note, 1. Good work goes on well when people have a mind to it. 2. The reproaches of enemies should rather quicken us to our duty than drive us from it.
entries.40432a84169b04ea248a6957df5841bbdd097847: <div eID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> But it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when Sanballat, and Tobiah, and the Arabians, and the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard that the walls of Jerusalem were made up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> that the breaches began to be stopped, then they were very wroth, <hi type="super">8</hi> And conspired all of them together to come <hi type="italic">and</hi> to fight against Jerusalem, and to hinder it. <hi type="super">9</hi> Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night, because of them. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall. <hi type="super">11</hi> And our adversaries said, They shall not know, neither see, till we come in the midst among them, and slay them, and cause the work to cease. <hi type="super">12</hi> And it came to pass, that when the Jews which dwelt by them came, they said unto us ten times, From all places whence ye shall return unto us <hi type="italic">they will be upon you.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore set I in the lower places behind the wall, <hi type="italic">and</hi> on the higher places, I even set the people after their families with their swords, their spears, and their bows. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, when our enemies heard that it was known unto us, and God had brought their counsel to nought, that we returned all of us to the wall, every one unto his work. <div eID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> I. The conspiracy which the Jews' enemies formed against them, to stay the building by slaying the builders. The conspirators were not only Sanballat and Tobiah, but other neighbouring people whom they had drawn into the plot. They flattered themselves with a fancy that the work would soon stand still of itself; but, when they heard that it went on a prospered, they were angry at the Jews for being so hasty to push the work forward and angry at themselves for being so slow in opposing it (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They were very wroth. Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, and their wrath, for it was cruel.</hi> Nothing would serve but they would <hi type="italic">fight against Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.4.8">v. 8</reference>. Why, what quarrel had they with the Jews? Had they done them any wrong? Or did they design them any? No, they lived peaceably by them; but it was merely out of envy and malice; they hated the Jews' piety, and were therefore vexed at their prosperity and sought their ruin. Observe, 1. How unanimous they were: <hi type="italic">They conspired all of them together,</hi> though of different interests among themselves, yet one in their opposition to the work of God. 2. How close they were; they said, "<hi type="italic">They shall not know, neither see,</hi> till we have them at our mercy." Thus they took crafty counsel, and digged deep to hide it from the Lord, and promised themselves security and success from the secresy of their management. 3. How cruel they were: <hi type="italic">We will come and slay them.</hi> If nothing less than the murder of the workmen will put a stop to the work, they will not stick at that; nay, it is their blood they thirst for, and they are glad of any pretence to glut themselves with it. 4. What the design was and how confident they were of success: it was to <hi type="italic">cause the work to cease</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">v. 11</reference>), and this they were confident that they should effect. The hindering of good work is that which bad men aim at and promise themselves; but good work is God's work, and it shall prosper. <div eID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> II. The discouragements which the builders themselves laboured under. At the very time when the adversaries said, Let us <hi type="italic">cause the work to cease,</hi> Judah said, "Let us even let it fall, for we are not able to go forward with it," <reference osisRef="Neh.4.10">v. 10</reference>. They represent the labourers as tired, and the remaining difficulties, even of that first part of their work, the removing of the rubbish, as insuperable, and therefore they think it advisable to desist for the present. Can Judah, that warlike valiant tribe, sneak thus? Active leading men have many times as much ado to grapple with the fears of their friends as with the terrors of their enemies. <div eID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> III. The information that was brought to Nehemiah of the enemies' designs, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.12">v. 12</reference>. There were <hi type="italic">Jews that dwelt by them,</hi> in the country, who, though they had not zeal enough to bring them to Jerusalem to help their brethren in building the wall, yet, having by their situation opportunity to discover the enemies' motions, had so much honesty and affection to the cause as to give intelligence of them; nay, that their intelligence might be the more credited, they came themselves to give it, and they said it ten times, repeating it as men in earnest, and under a concern, and the report was confirmed by many witnesses. The intelligence they gave is expressed abruptly, and finds work for the critics to make out the sense of it, which perhaps is designed to intimate that they gave this intelligence as men out of breath and in confusion, whose very looks would make up the deficiencies of their words. I think it may be read, without supplying any thing: "<hi type="italic">Whatever place you turn to, they are against us,</hi> so that you have need to be upon your guard on all sides," Note, God has many ways of bringing to light, and so bringing to nought, the devices and designs of his and his church's enemies. Even the cold and feeble Jews that contentedly dwell by them shall be made to serve as spies upon them; nay, rather than fail, <hi type="italic">a bird of the air shall carry their voice.</hi> <div eID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> IV. The pious and prudent methods which Nehemiah, hereupon, took to baffle the design, and to secure his work and workmen. <div eID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> 1. It is said (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.14">v. 14</reference>) he <hi type="italic">looked.</hi> (1.) He looked up, engaged God for him, and put himself and his cause under the divine protection (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">We made our prayer unto our God.</hi> That was the way of this good man, and should be our way; all his cares, all his griefs, all his fears, he spread before God, and thereby made himself easy. This was the first thing he did; before he used any means, he made his prayer to God, for with him we must always begin. (2.) He looked about him. Having prayed, he <hi type="italic">set a watch against them.</hi> The instructions Christ has given us in our spiritual warfare agree with this example, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.41">Matt. xxvi. 41</reference>. <hi type="italic">Watch and pray.</hi> If we think to secure ourselves by prayer only, without watchfulness, we are slothful and tempt God; if by watchfulness, without prayer, we are proud and slight God; and, either way, we forfeit his protection. <div eID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe, (1.) How he posted the guards, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">In the lower places</hi> he set them <hi type="italic">behind the wall,</hi> that they might annoy the enemy over it, as a breast-work; but <hi type="italic">in the higher places,</hi> where the wall was raised to its full height, he set them upon it, that from the top of it they might throw down stones or darts upon the heads of the assailants: he set them <hi type="italic">after their families,</hi> that mutual relation might engage them to mutual assistance. (2.) How he animated and encouraged the people, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.14">v. 14</reference>. He observed even the nobles and rulers themselves, as well as the rest of the people, to be in a great consternation upon the intelligence that was brought them, and ready to conclude that they were all undone, by which their hands were weakened both for work and war, and therefore, he endeavours to silence their fears. "Come," says he, "<hi type="italic">be not afraid of them,</hi> but behave yourselves valiantly, considering, [1.] Whom you fight under. You cannot have a better captain: <hi type="italic">Remember the Lord, who is great and terrible;</hi> you think your enemies <hi type="italic">great and terrible,</hi> but what are they in comparison with God, especially in opposition to him? He is great above them to control them, and will be terrible to them when he comes to reckon with them." Those that with an eye of faith see the church's God to be great and terrible will see the church's enemies to be mean and despicable. The reigning fear of God is the best antidote against the ensnaring fear of man. He that is afraid of <hi type="italic">a man that shall die forgets the Lord his Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. lxxiv. 12, 13</reference>. [2.] "Whom you fight for. You cannot have a better cause; you fight for <hi type="italic">your brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.8">Ps. cxxii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">your sons, and your daughters.</hi> All that is dear to you in their world lies at stake; therefore <hi type="italic">behave yourselves valiantly.</hi>" <div eID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> V. The happy disappointment which this gave to the enemies, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.15">v. 15</reference>. When they found that their design was discovered, and that the Jews were upon their guard, they concluded that it was to no purpose to attempt any thing, but that <hi type="italic">God had brought their counsel to nought.</hi> They knew they could not gain their point but by surprise, and, if their plot was known, it was quashed. The Jews hereupon <hi type="italic">returned every one to his work,</hi> with so much the more cheerfulness because they saw plainly that God owned it and owned them in the doing of it. Note, God's care of our safety should engage and encourage us to go on with vigour in our duty. As soon as ever a danger is over let us <hi type="italic">return to our work,</hi> and trust God another time.
entries.fa8db829039ff04cb69ec387b948c5260fe4c590: <div eID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Precautions of Nehemiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 445.)</title> <div sID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass from that time forth, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the half of my servants wrought in the work, and the other half of them held both the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons; and the rulers <hi type="italic">were</hi> behind all the house of Judah. <hi type="super">17</hi> They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, <hi type="italic">every one</hi> with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other <hi type="italic">hand</hi> held a weapon. <hi type="super">18</hi> For the builders, every one had his sword girded by his side, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> builded. And he that sounded the trumpet <hi type="italic">was</hi> by me. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, The work <hi type="italic">is</hi> great and large, and we are separated upon the wall, one far from another. <hi type="super">20</hi> In what place <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us. <hi type="super">21</hi> So we laboured in the work: and half of them held the spears from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared. <hi type="super">22</hi> Likewise at the same time said I unto the people, Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, that in the night they may be a guard to us, and labour on the day. <hi type="super">23</hi> So neither I, nor my brethren, nor my servants, nor the men of the guard which followed me, none of us put off our clothes, <hi type="italic">saving that</hi> every one put them off for washing. <div eID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8793" type="x-p"/> When the builders had so far reason to think the design of the enemies broken <hi type="italic">as to return to their work,</hi> yet they were not so secure as to lay down their arms, knowing how restless and unwearied they were in their attempts, and that, if one design failed, they would be hatching another. Thus must we watch always against our spiritual enemies, and not expect that our warfare will be accomplished till our work is. See what course Nehemiah took, that the people might hold themselves in a readiness, in case there should be an attack. 1. While one half were at work, the other half were under their arms, holding <hi type="italic">spears, and shields, and bows,</hi> not only for themselves but for the labourers too, who would immediately quit their work, and betake themselves to their weapons, upon the first alarm, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.16">v. 16</reference>. It is probable that they changed services at stated hours, which would relieve the fatigue of both, and particularly would be an ease to the <hi type="italic">bearers of burdens,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">strength</hi> had <hi type="italic">decayed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.10">v. 10</reference>); while they held the weapons, they were eased and yet not idle. Thus dividing their time between the trowels and the spears, they are said to <hi type="italic">work with one hand</hi> and hold their weapons <hi type="italic">with the other</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.17">v. 17</reference>), which cannot be understood literally, for the work would require both hands; but it intimates that they were equally employed in both. Thus must we work out our salvation with the weapons of our warfare in our hand; for in every duty we must expect to meet with opposition from our spiritual enemies, against whom we must still be <hi type="italic">fighting the good fight of faith.</hi> 2. Every builder had a sword by his side (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.18">v. 18</reference>), which he could carry without hindering his labour. The word of God is the sword of the Spirit, which we ought to have always at hand and never to seek, both in our labours and in our conflicts as Christians. 3. Care was taken both to get and give early notice of the approach of the enemy, in case they should endeavour to surprise them. Nehemiah kept a trumpeter always by him to sound an alarm, upon the first intimation of danger. The work was large, and the builders were dispersed; for in all parts of the wall they were labouring at the same time. Nehemiah continually walked round to oversee the work and encourage the workmen, and so would have speedy intelligence if the enemy made an attack, of which, by sound of trumpet, he would soon give notice to all, and they must immediately repair to him with a full assurance that their <hi type="italic">God</hi> would <hi type="italic">fight for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.4.18-Neh.4.20">v. 18-20</reference>. When they acted as workmen, it was requisite they should be dispersed wherever there was work to do; but when as soldiers it was requisite they should come into close order, and be found in a body. Thus should the labourers in Christ's building be ready to unite against a common foe. 4. The inhabitants of the villages were ordered to lodge within Jerusalem, with their servants, not only that they might be the nearer to their work in the morning, but that they might be ready to help in case of an attack in the night, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.22">v. 22</reference>. The strength of a city lies more in its hands than in its walls; secure them, and God's blessing upon them, and be secure. 5. Nehemiah himself, and all his men, kept closely to their business. The spears were held up, with the sight of them to terrify the enemy, not only from sun to sun, but from twilight to twilight every day, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.21">v. 21</reference>. Thus ought we to be always upon our guard against our spiritual enemies, not only (as here) while <hi type="italic">it is light,</hi> but when <hi type="italic">it is dark,</hi> for they are the <hi type="italic">rulers of the darkness of this world.</hi> Nay, so very intent was Nehemiah upon his work, and so fast did he hold his servants to it, that while the heat of the business lasted neither he himself nor his attendants went into bed, but every night lay and slept in their clothes (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.23">v. 23</reference>), except that they shifted them now and then, either for cleanliness or in a case of ceremonial pollution. It was a sign that their heart was upon their work when they could not find time to dress and undress, but resolved they would be at all times ready for service. Good work is likely to go on successfully when those that labour in it thus make a business of it.  <chapter eID="Neh.4"/> <div eID="gen8793" type="x-p"/>

entries.89480fda0d3ce310676207dd595fa6b9cc06a613: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4320"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.4.1-Neh.4.6">Ne 4:1-6</reference>. While the Enemies Scoff, Nehemiah Prays to God, and Continues the Work.</title> <div sID="gen6266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4320"/><hi type="bold">1. when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth--</hi>The Samaritan faction showed their bitter animosity to the Jews on discovering the systematic design of refortifying Jerusalem. Their opposition was confined at first to scoffs and insults, in heaping which the governors made themselves conspicuous, and circulated all sorts of disparaging reflections that might increase the feelings of hatred and contempt for them in their own party. The weakness of the Jews in respect of wealth and numbers, the absurdity of their purpose apparently to reconstruct the walls and celebrate the feast of dedication in one day, the idea of raising the walls on their old foundations, as well as using the charred and mouldering debris of the ruins as the materials for the restored buildings, and the hope of such a parapet as they could raise being capable of serving as a fortress of defense--these all afforded fertile subjects of hostile ridicule. <div eID="gen6266" type="x-p"/>
entries.e593443825bd7442cfa73dbcca3ec378877fffbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4321"/><div sID="gen6267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4321"/><hi type="bold">3. if a fox go up--</hi>The foxes were mentioned because they were known to infest in great numbers the ruined and desolate places in the mount and city of Zion (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.18">La 5:18</reference>). <div eID="gen6267" type="x-p"/>
entries.07fb7dc726b74bf74f8b725be76a9d9cc080bb1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4322"/><div sID="gen6268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4322"/><hi type="bold">4-5. Hear, O our God; for we are despised--</hi>The imprecations invoked here may seem harsh, cruel, and vindictive; but it must be remembered that Nehemiah and his friends regarded those Samaritan leaders as enemies to the cause of God and His people, and therefore as deserving to be visited with heavy judgments. The prayer, therefore, is to be considered as emanating from hearts in which neither hatred, revenge, nor any inferior passion, but a pious and patriotic zeal for the glory of God and the success of His cause, held the ascendant sway. <div eID="gen6268" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfa836f22d2337d36a630272f16712131dc11448: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4323"/><div sID="gen6269" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4323"/><hi type="bold">6. all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof--</hi>The whole circuit of the wall had been distributed in sections to various companies of the people, and was completed to the half of the intended height. <div eID="gen6269" type="x-p"/>
entries.24b8b89e7300ebf56441a918d949f0ea433d8554: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4324"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.4.7-Neh.4.23">Ne 4:7-23</reference>. He Sets a Watch.</title> <div sID="gen6270" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4324"/><hi type="bold">7-21. But ... when Sanballat ... heard that the walls ... were made up, and ... the breaches ... stopped--</hi>The rapid progress of the fortifications, despite all their predictions to the contrary, goaded the Samaritans to frenzy. So they, dreading danger from the growing greatness of the Jews, formed a conspiracy to surprise them, demolish their works, and disperse or intimidate the builders. The plot being discovered, Nehemiah adopted the most energetic measures for ensuring the common safety, as well as the uninterrupted building of the walls. Hitherto the governor, for the sake of despatch, had set all his attendants and guards on the work--now half of them were withdrawn to be constantly in arms. The workmen labored with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other; and as, in so large a circuit, they were far removed from each other, Nehemiah (who was night and day on the spot, and, by his pious exhortations and example, animated the minds of his people) kept a trumpeter by his side, so that, on any intelligence of a surprise being brought to him, an alarm might be immediately sounded, and assistance rendered to the most distant detachment of their brethren. By these vigilant precautions, the counsels of the enemy were defeated, and the work was carried on apace. God, when He has important public work to do, never fails to raise up instruments for accomplishing it, and in the person of Nehemiah, who, to great natural acuteness and energy added fervent piety and heroic devotion, He provided a leader, whose high qualities fitted him for the demands of the crisis. Nehemiah's vigilance anticipated every difficulty, his prudent measures defeated every obstruction, and with astonishing rapidity this Jerusalem was made again "a city fortified." <chapter eID="Neh.4"/>

entries.8038f09c17a49308b7f5fa33f3641d4505650504: <div eID="gen15009" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15010" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15011" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15011" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15010" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15012" type="x-p"/> Sanballat and Tobiah mock the Jews, and endeavor to prevent the completing of the wall, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.1-Neh.4.3">Neh 4:1-3</reference>. Nehemiah prays against them, and the people complete one half of the wall, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.4-Neh.4.6">Neh 4:4-6</reference>. The Arabians, Ammonites, and Ashdodites, conspire together, and come to fight against the Jews, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.7">Neh 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.8">Neh 4:8</reference>. The Jews commend themselves to God, and determine to fight for their lives and liberties; on hearing of which their enemies are disheartened, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.9-Neh.4.16">Neh 4:9-16</reference>. The Jews divide themselves into two bands; one half working, and the other standing ready armed to meet their enemies. Even the workmen are obliged to arm themselves, while employed in building, for fear of their enemies, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.17">Neh 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.18">Neh 4:18</reference>. Nehemiah uses all precautions to prevent a surprise; and all labor with great fervor in the work, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.19-Neh.4.22">Neh 4:19-22</reference>.
entries.8e265a59809b5cc33c8ad6f182004ca0df584e19: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15013" type="x-p"/> The army of Samaria - As he was governor, he had the command of the army, and he wished to excite the soldiers to second his views against Nehemiah and his men. <div eID="gen15013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15014" type="x-p"/> What do these feeble Jews? - We may remark here, in general, that the enemies of God's work endeavor by all means to discredit and destroy it, and those who are employed in it. <div eID="gen15014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15015" type="x-p"/> 1. They despise the workmen: What do these feeble Jews? <div eID="gen15015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15016" type="x-p"/> 2. They endeavor to turn all into ridicule: Will they fortify themselves? <div eID="gen15016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15017" type="x-p"/> 3. They have recourse to lying: If a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall. <div eID="gen15017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15018" type="x-p"/> 4. They sometimes use fair but deceitful speeches; see <reference osisRef="Neh.6.2">Neh 6:2</reference>, etc.
entries.2337869e98cc9f50d01da3ce208b9cb677d5c7ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15019" type="x-p"/> Turn their reproach upon their own head - A prayer of this kind, understood literally, is not lawful for any Christian. Jesus, our great master, has said, "Love your enemies; do good to them that hate you; and pray for them that despitefully use you." Such sayings as the above are excusable in the mouth of a Jew, under severe irritation. See the next verse, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.5">Neh 4:5</reference> (note).
entries.c91fdcb65be2bf8384d8553af8ad382777223f7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15020" type="x-p"/> Let not their sin be blotted out - These are the most terrible imprecations; but probably we should understand them as declaratory, for the same form of the verb, in the Hebrew, is used as precative and imperative. Turn their reproach - Their reproach shall be turned. Give them for a prey - They shall be given for a prey. Cover not their iniquity - Their iniquity shall not be covered. Let not their sin be blotted out - Their sin shall not be blotted out. All who know the genius of the Hebrew language, know that the future tense is used to express all these senses. Besides, we may rest assured that Nehemiah's curses, or declaration of God's judgments, had respect only to their bodies, and to their life: not to their souls and the world to come. And then they amount to no more than this: What a man soweth that he shall reap.
entries.e692d21b70793e1970f7aa3d8c9be36a52ff6431: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15021" type="x-p"/> For the people had a mind to work - The original is very emphatic: ויהי לב לעם לעשות vayehi leb leam laasoth, "For the people had a heart to work." Their hearts were engaged in it; and where the heart is engaged, the work of God goes on well. The whole of this 6th verse is omitted by the Septuagint.
entries.4cff892a9035b113e5476f0fd1cd41a53e1855cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15022" type="x-p"/> The walls of Jerusalem were made up - That is, they were made up to the half height of the wall; for the preceding verse seems to intimate that the whole wall was thus far built; not half of the wall completed, but the whole wall built to half its height.
entries.a0e490256a44d07f796b5d3efa4325d2e8ef1a35: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15023" type="x-p"/> We made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch - The strongest confidence in the protection and favor of God does not preclude the use of all or any of the means of self-preservation and defense which his providence has put in our power. While God works in us to will and to do, we should proceed to willing, through the power he has given us to will; and we should proceed to action, through the power he has given us to act. We cannot will, but through God's power; we cannot act, but through God's strength. The power, and the use of it, are two distinct things. We may have the power to will, and not will; and we may have the power to do, and not act: therefore, says the apostle, seeing God has wrought in you these powers, see that You Work Out Your Own salvation, with fear and trembling.
entries.ca5885818275550ae1d2ade8b7dfe2ac664890f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15024" type="x-p"/> The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed - They worked both day and night, scarcely ever putting off their clothes, except for the purpose of being washed, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.21">Neh 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.23">Neh 4:23</reference>. <div eID="gen15024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15025" type="x-p"/> Much rubbish - The ruins they were obliged to clear away, before they could dig the foundation for a new wall: and in this labor they were nearly exhausted; see <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh 5:15</reference>.
entries.9a4a9fbd406769d6e864182f08f6f5f60d063a25: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen15025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15026" type="x-p"/> From all places whence ye shall return unto us - This verse is extremely difficult. Our translators have supplied the words, they will be upon you, which have nothing correspondent in the Hebrew. The Septuagint have given a good sense, Αναβαινουσιν εκ παντων των τοπων εφ' ἡμας, They come up from all places against us. The sense appears to be this: the Jews which dwelt among the Samaritans, etc., came often to Nehemiah from all quarters, where they sojourned, and told him the designs of his enemies against him: therefore, he set people with their swords, spears, and bows, to defend the walls. It is probable that instead of תשובו tashubu, "ye shall return," we should read חשבו chashebu, "they designed or meditated." This word is very similar to the other, and makes the sense very clear. "The Jews who dwelt among them told us frequently, from all places, what they designed against us." For this reading Houbigant, Michaelis and Dath contend. But this various reading is not found in any MS., and is not countenanced by any of the versions. See <reference osisRef="Neh.4.15">Neh 4:15</reference>.
entries.2cf173a06cae295d05ec89196a13c98b8b5ed3db: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15027" type="x-p"/> Be not ye afraid of them - Are they more terrible or stronger than God? <div eID="gen15027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15028" type="x-p"/> Fight for your brethren - Your own countrymen, who worship the same God, and are come from the same stock; your sons, whom they wish to slay or lead into captivity; your daughters and wives, whom they wish to deflower and defile; and your houses, which they wish to seize and occupy as their own. They had every thing at stake; and therefore they must fight pro aris et focis, for their religion, their lives, and their property. A people thus interested, who once take up the sword, can never be conquered. <div eID="gen15028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15029" type="x-p"/> There is an address made to the Greeks by their leader in Aeschylus, Pers. ver. 402, similar to this, to excite them against the Persians: - - Ω Παιδες Ἑλληνων, ιτε, Ελευθερουτε πατριδ,ελευθερουτε δε Παιδας, γυνιακας, θεων ρε πατρῳων ἑδη, Θηκας τε προγονων· νυν ὑπερ παντων αγων. " - Sons of the Greeks, go on! <div eID="gen15029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15030" type="x-p"/> Free now your country, and your children free; <div eID="gen15030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15031" type="x-p"/> Your wives, the temples of your fathers' gods, <div eID="gen15031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15032" type="x-p"/> And dear abodes of farthest ancestors: - <div eID="gen15032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15033" type="x-p"/> Now strike the blow for all!" <div eID="gen15033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15034" type="x-p"/> J. B. B. C.
entries.d9ac45dd5314e95271a2361e6367463d782ebcb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> Their counsel to naught - The word counsel used here countenances the emendation in the 12th verse.
entries.bae0319fd0c28488b124fb094e462d2e6ebdb747: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15036" type="x-p"/> Half - wrought in the work - This is no unusual thing, even in the present day, in Palestine: people sowing their seed are often attended by an armed man, to prevent the Arabs from robbing them of their seed, which they will not fail to do if not protected. <div eID="gen15036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> Habergeons - In the Franco-Gallic, hautbergon signifies a coat of mail; but as in Teutonic hais signifies the neck, and bergen, to cover or defend; it may be considered rather as signifying a breastplate, or armor for the breast.
entries.a385ef20aa219714c76d8f521e2a17ef32ed8587: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> With one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon - That is, he had his arms at hand, and was as fully prepared to fight as to work. So Ovid, Epist. xi., Canace Macario, ver. 1: - <div eID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15039" type="x-p"/> Si qua tamen caecis errabunt scripta lituris, <div eID="gen15039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15040" type="x-p"/> Oblitus a dominae caede libellus erit: <div eID="gen15040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15041" type="x-p"/> Dextra tenet calamum; strictum tenet altera ferrum: <div eID="gen15041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> Et jacet in gremio charta soluta meo. <div eID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> If streaming blood my fatal letter stain, <div eID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> Imagine, ere you read, the writer slain. <div eID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> One hand the sword, and one the pen employs, <div eID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> And in my lap the ready paper lies. <div eID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> By this mode of speech Canace does not intimate to her brother Macarius, that she actually held the sword in one hand while she held the pen in the other, but that she had it ready to slay herself as soon as she had written the epistle.
entries.078d59c6dcdafdc93d0c77c90249cb8aac7f48b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> Ye hear the sound of the trumpet - As the walls were very extensive, and the workmen consequently much scattered, their enemies might easily attack and destroy them successively, he therefore ordered them all to work as near to each other as they could; and himself, who was everywhere surveying the work, kept a trumpeter always with him, who was to sound when the enemy approached; and all were instantly to run to the place where they heard the sound.
entries.a29d4bb597b72b0fb1c154872c490ef6b1f68813: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem - The country people were accustomed, after their day's labor, to return to their families; now being so formidably threatened, he obliged them all to sleep in Jerusalem, that they might be ready, in case of attack, to help their brethren. All this man's arrangements were wise and judicious.
entries.a88afbdc02aef55eb4f2bf0bf82092ce7f3825d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> None of us put off our clothes, saving that every one put them off for washing - The Hebrew for all this is only אין אנחנו פשטים בגדינו איש שלחו המים ein anachnu poshetim begadeynu ish shilcho hammayim; which Montanus translates, Non nos exuentes vestes nostras, vir missile suum aquas; "We, not putting off our garments, a man his dart to the waters." Of this latter clause what sense can be made? Let us hear what the ancient versions say. <div eID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, Unusquisque tantum nudabatur ad baptismum, "Every one stripped himself for the bath." <div eID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint omit the latter part of this clause, And there was none of us who put off his garments. <div eID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> The Syriac, "None of us put off his clothes for a month each in his turn. <div eID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> The Arabic, "Nor did we put off our clothes, but with our arms, at the end of a month." <div eID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15056" type="x-p"/> There is a remarkable reading in one of De Rossi's MSS. אין אנחנו פשטים בגדינו משלחהעל המים, We did not lay aside our garments, but in order to send them to the washing. This is most likely the sense of the place. <div eID="gen15056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> It is curious to see how our old versions translate the place. <div eID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15058" type="x-p"/> Coverdale: We put never of our clothes, so much as to wash ourselves. - 1535. <div eID="gen15058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15059" type="x-p"/> Becke: We put never of our clothes, so muche as to washe ourselves. - 1549. <div eID="gen15059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> Cardmarden: We put never of oure clothes no more than the other dyd theyr harnesse, save onely bycause of the water. - 1566. <div eID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> This shows how all interpreters have been puzzled with this vexatious clause. <div eID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15062" type="x-p"/> The reading from De Rossi's MS., given above, is the most likely to be the true one, because it gives a good sense, which cannot be found in the Hebrew text as it now stands. The general meaning is sufficiently evident; they worked nearly day and night, only had their hours by turns for repose; this did not permit them time sufficient to undress themselves in order to take regular sleep, therefore they only put off their clothes when they were obliged to get them washed.  <chapter eID="Neh.4"/> <div eID="gen15062" type="x-p"/>

entries.b3f9c8405378a095636146b3131f2ea9ef1cfec1: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.1-Neh.4.2">Neh 4:1-2</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_3:33-34)<hi type="italic">The ridicule of Tobiah and Sanballat</hi>. - As soon as Sanballat heard that we were building (בּנים, <hi type="italic">partic</hi>., expresses not merely the resolve or desire to build, but also the act of commencing), he was wroth and indignant, and vented his anger by ridiculing the Jews, saying before his brethren, i.e., the rulers of his people, and the army of Samaria (חיל, like <reference osisRef="Esth.1.3">Est 1:3</reference>; 2Ki 18:17), - in other words, saying publicly before his associates and subordinates, - “What do these feeble Jews? will they leave it to themselves? will they sacrifice? will they finish it to-day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps that are burned?” עשׂים מה, not, What will they do? (Bertheau), for the participle is present, and does not stand for the future; but, What are they doing? The form אמלל, withered, powerless, occurs here only. The subject of the four succeeding interrogative sentences must be the same. And this is enough to render inadmissible the explanation offered by older expositors of להם היעזבוּ: Will they leave to them, viz., will the neighbouring nations or the royal prefects allow them to build? Here, as in the case of the following verbs, the subject can only be the Jews. Hence Ewald seeks, both here and in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.8">Neh 4:8</reference>, to give to the verb עזב the meaning to shelter: Will they make a shelter for themselves, i.e., will they fortify the town? But this is quite arbitrary. Bertheau more correctly compares the passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>, אלהים על עזבנוּ, we leave it to God; but incorrectly infers that here also we must supply אלהים על, and that, Will they leave to themselves? means, Will they commit the matter to God. This mode of completing the sense, however, can by no means be justified; and Bertheau’s conjecture, that the Jews now assembling in Jerusalem, before commencing the work itself, instituted a devotional solemnity which Sanballat was ridiculing, is incompatible with the correct rendering of the participle. עזב construed with ל means to leave, to commit a matter to any one, like <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>, and the sense is: Will they leave the building of the fortified walls to themselves? i.e., Do they think they are able with their poor resources to carry out this great work? This is appropriately followed by the next question: Will they sacrifice? i.e., bring sacrifices to obtain God’s miraculous assistance? The ridicule lies in the circumstance that Sanballat neither credited the Jews with ability to carry out the work, nor believed in the overruling providence of the God whom the Jews worshipped, and therefore casts scorn by היזבּחוּ both upon the faith of the Jews in their God and upon the living God Himself. As these two questions are internally connected, so also are the two following, by which Sanballat casts a doubt upon the possibility of the work being executed. Will they finish (the work) on this day, i.e., to-day, directly? The meaning is: Is this a matter to be as quickly executed as if it were the work of a single day? The last question is: Have they even the requisite materials? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish which are burnt? The building-stone of Jerusalem was limestone, which gets softened by fire, losing its durability, and, so to speak, its vitality. This explains the use of the verb חיּה, to revive, bestow strength and durability upon the softened crumbled stones, to fit the stones into a new building (Ges. <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.). The construction שׂרוּפות והמּה is explained by the circumstance that אבנים is by its form masculine, but by its meaning feminine, and that המּה agrees with the form אבנים.
entries.904a979044914cb9edbefd44c7d5399cf00a387d: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.3">Neh 4:3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_3:35) <div eID="gen6536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6537" type="x-p"/> Tobiah the Ammonite, standing near Sanballat, and joining in in his raillery, adds: “Even that which they build, if a fox go up he will break their stone wall;” i.e., even if they build up walls, the light footsteps of the stealthy fox will suffice to tread them down, and to make breaches in their work.
entries.7df351e7f4dd26f8b7ebb0add7e1317c61eb5ebd: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.4-Neh.4.5">Neh 4:4-5</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_3:36-37) <div eID="gen6537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6538" type="x-p"/> When Nehemiah heard of these contemptuous words, he committed the matter to God, entreating Him to hear how they (the Jews) were become a scorn, i.e., a subject of contempt, to turn the reproach of the enemies upon their own head, and to give them up the plunder in a land of captivity, i.e., in a land in which they would dwell as captives. He supplicates, moreover, that God would not cover, i.e., forgive (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.3">Psa 85:3</reference>), their iniquity, and that their sin might not be blotted out from before His face, i.e., might not remain unpunished, “for they have provoked to wrath before the builders,” i.e., openly challenged the wrath of God, by despising Him before the builders, so that they heard it. הכעים without an object, spoken of provoking the divine wrath by grievous sins; comp. 2Ki 21:6 with 2Ch 33:6.
entries.d894f7cbba14ad44701af03d846815025f8f79a8: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.6-Neh.4.8">Neh 4:6-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_3:38-4:1-2) <div eID="gen6538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6539" type="x-p"/> The Jews continued to build without heeding the ridicule of their enemies, ”and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof,” i.e., the wall was so far repaired throughout its whole circumference, that no breach or gap was left up to half its height; “and the people had a heart to work,” i.e., the restoration went on so quickly because the people had a mind to work.<hi type="italic">The attempts of the enemies to hinder the work by force, and Nehemiah’s precautions against them</hi>. - When the enemies learnt that the restoration of the wall was evidently getting on, they conspired together to fight against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.1">Neh 4:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.4.2">Neh 4:2</reference>). The Jews then prayed to God, and set a watch (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.3">Neh 4:3</reference>). When the courage of the people began to fail, and their enemies spread a report of sudden attack being imminent, Nehemiah furnished the people on the wall with weapons, and encouraged the nobles and rulers to fight boldly for their brethren, their children, and their possessions (vv. 4-8). The Arabians, Ammonites, and Ashdodites are here enumerated as enemies, besides Sanballat and Tobiah (vv. 2, 10, 19). The Arabians were incited to hostilities against the Jews by Geshem (vv. 11, 19), and the Ammonites by Tobiah; the Ashdodites, the inhabitants of the city and territory of Ashdod, in the coast district of Philistia, were perhaps encouraged to renew their old hatred of Judah by Sanballat the Horonite. When these enemies heard that the walls of Jerusalem were bandaged, i.e., that the breaches and damages in the wall were repaired, they were filled with wrath. The biblical expression, to lay on a bandage, here and <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.13">2Ch 24:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jer 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">Jer 30:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.6">Jer 33:6</reference>, is derived from the healing of wounds by means of a bandage, and is explained by the sentence following: that the breaches began to be closed or stopped. The enemies conspired together to march against Jerusalem and injure it. לו, because the people of the town are meant. תּועה occurs but once more, viz., in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>, in the sense of error; here it signifies <hi type="italic">calamities</hi>, for, as Aben Ezra well remarks, <hi type="italic">qui in angustiis constitutus est, est velut errans, qui nescit quid agat quove se vertat.</hi>
entries.d9b84d64e7c185e2c39125427a63b484889f5868: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.9">Neh 4:9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:3) <div eID="gen6539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6540" type="x-p"/> The Jews, on the other hand, made preparation by prayer, and by setting a watch (משׁמר, comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.7.3">Neh 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.30">Neh 13:30</reference>) day and night. We, viz., Nehemiah and the superintendents of the work, prayed and set a watch עליהם, against them, to ward off a probable attack. מפּניהם, for fear of them, comp. Neh 4:10.
entries.2ea024b8ce08762b5ee108482ae006fb22b350ec: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.10">Neh 4:10</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:4) <div eID="gen6540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6541" type="x-p"/> The placing of the watch day and night, and the continuous labour, must have pressed heavily upon the people; therefore Judah said: “The strength of the bearers of burdens fails, and there is much rubbish; we are not able to build the wall.” That is to say, the labour is beyond our power, we cannot continue it.
entries.c37881e6ca15bfcbbcc3dcc228e58bdc58466070: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">Neh 4:11</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:5) <div eID="gen6541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6542" type="x-p"/> Their discouragement was increased by the words of their enemies, who said: They (the Jews) shall not know nor see, till we come in the midst among them, and slay them, and cause the work to cease.
entries.3d64102d3556e954038c7200e98e009bcad82ffd: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.12">Neh 4:12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:6-7) <div eID="gen6542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6543" type="x-p"/> When, therefore, the Jews who dwelt near them, i.e., in the neighbourhood of the adversaries, and heard their words, came to Jerusalem, “and said to us ten times (i.e., again and again), that from all places ye must return to us, then I placed,” etc. Jews came from all places to Jerusalem, and summoned those who were building there to return home, for adversaries were surrounding the community on all sides: Sanballat and the Samaritans on the north, the Ammonites on the east, the Arabians on the south, and the Philistines (Ashdodites) on the west. אשׁר before תּשׁוּבוּ introduces their address, instead of כּי; being thus used, e.g., before longer speeches, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20">1Sa 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.4">2Sa 1:4</reference>; and for כּי generally, throughout the later books, in conformity to Aramaean usage. “Return to us” (על שׁוּב, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.9">2Ch 30:9</reference>, for אל שׁוּב), said the Jews who came from all quarters to Jerusalem to their fellow-townsmen, who from Jericho, Gibeon, and Tekoa (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.2-Neh.3.3">Neh 3:2-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.7">Neh 3:7</reference>) were working on the wall of Jerusalem. These words express their fear lest those who were left at home, especially the defenceless women, children, and aged men, should be left without protection against the attacks of enemies, if their able-bodied men remained any longer in Jerusalem to take part in the building of the wall.
entries.b4fbb51a2d579d864e5b35c1cf79d25c4143d456: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.13">Neh 4:13</reference> <div eID="gen6543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6544" type="x-p"/> Hebrew_Bible_<hi type="italic">4:7</hi> is hardly intelligible. We translate it: Then I placed at the lowest places behind the wall, at the dried-up places, I (even) placed the people, after their families, with their swords, their spears, and their bows. למּקום מתּחתּיּות is a stronger expression for למּקום מתּחת when used to indicate position, and מן points out the direction. The sense is: at the lowest places from behind the wall. בּצּחחים gives the nature of the places where the people were placed with arms. צחיח and צחיחה mean a dry or bare place exposed to the heat of the sun: bare, uncovered, or empty places, perhaps bare hills, whence approaching foes might be discerned at a distance. The second ואעמיד is but a reiteration of the verb, for the sake of combining it with its object, from which the ואעמיד at the beginning of the verse was too far removed by the circumstantial description of the locality.<note placement="foot">Bertheau considers the text corrupt, regarding the word מתּחתּיּות as the object of אעמיד, and alters it into מחשׁבות or חשּׁבנות, engines for hurling missiles (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.15">2Ch 26:15</reference>), or into מטחיּות (a word of this own invention), instruments for hurling. But not only is this conjecture critically inadmissible, it also offers no appropriate sense. The lxx reads the text as we do, and merely renders בצחחיים conjecturally by ἐν τοῖς σκεπεινοῖς. Besides, it is not easy to see how חשׁבנות could have arisen from a false reading of מתחתיות; and it should be remembered that מחשׁבות does not mean a machine for hurling, while מטחתייות is a mere fabrication. To this must be added, that such machines are indeed placed upon the walls of a fortress to hurl down stones and projectiles upon assaulting foes, and not behind the walls, where they could only be used to demolish the walls, and so facilitate the taking of the town by the enemy.</note>
entries.652ebc133f8637468a509131a8cd09b6bd98f73e: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.14">Neh 4:14</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:8) “And I looked, and rose up, and said.” These words can only mean: When I saw the people thus placed with their weapons, I went to them, and said to the nobles, etc., “Be not afraid of them (the enemies); remember the Lord, the great and the terrible,” who will fight for you against your enemies (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.22">Deu 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.20.3">Deu 20:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">Deu 31:6</reference>), “and fight ye for your brethren, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your houses,” whom the enemies would destroy.  (Hebrew_Bible_4:9-17) <div eID="gen6544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6545" type="x-p"/> Thus was the design of the enemy circumvented, and the Jews returned to their work on the wall, which they had forsaken to betake themselves to their weapons. The manner in which they resumed their building work was, that one half held weapons, and the other half laboured with weapons in hand.
entries.dc42a16edd2f3dddcb6eb5aa6bac6438c4b06a8a: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.15">Neh 4:15</reference> <div eID="gen6545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6546" type="x-p"/> When our enemies heard that it (their intention) was known to us, and (that) God had brought their counsel to nought (through the measures with which we had met it), we returned all of us to the wall, every one to his work. The conclusion does not begin till ונּשׁוב, האל ויּפר belonging to the premiss, in continuation of נודא כּי.
entries.3bedc22894a57e79073aca8c126339809c8a723b: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.16-Neh.4.18">Neh 4:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen6546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6547" type="x-p"/> From that day the half of my servants wrought at the work, and the other half of them held the spears and shields, the bows and the armour, i.e., carried the arms. The servants of Nehemiah are his personal retinue, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.17">Neh 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.10">Neh 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.16">Neh 5:16</reference>, namely, Jews placed at his disposal as Pechah for official purposes. The ו before הרמחים was probably placed before this word, instead of before the המּגנּים following, by a clerical error; for if it stood before the latter also, it might be taken in the sense of <hi type="italic">et</hi> - <hi type="italic">et</hi>. מצזיקים, instead of being construed with בּ, is in the accusative, as also in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">Neh 4:11</reference>, and even in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.23">Jer 6:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.41.9">Isa 41:9</reference>, Isa 41:13. Unnecessary and unsuitable is the conjecture of Bertheau, that the word בּרמחים originally stood after מצזיקים, and that a fresh sentence begins with והרמחים: and the other half held the spears; and the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the armour, and the rulers, were behind the whole house of Judah, - a strange combination, which places the weapons and rulers behind the house of Judah. Besides, of the circumstance of the weapons being placed behind the builders, so that they might at any moment seize them, we not only read nothing in the text; but in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">Neh 4:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.4.12">Neh 4:12</reference> just the contrary, viz., that the builders wrought with one hand, and with the other held a weapon. “The rulers were behind all the house of Judah,” i.e., each was behind his own people who were employed on the work, to encourage them in their labour, and, in case of attack, to lead them against the enemy. - In <reference osisRef="Neh.4.11">Neh 4:11</reference> בּחומה הבּונים is prefixed after the manner of a title. With respect to those who built the wall, both the bearers of burdens were lading with the one hand of each workman, and holding a weapon with the other, and the builders were building each with his sword girt on his side. The ו prefixed to הנּשׂאים and הבּנים means both; and בסּבל נשׂא, bearers of burdens, who cleared away the rubbish, and worked as labourers. These, at all events, could do their work with one hand, which would suffice for emptying rubbish into baskets, and for carrying material in handle baskets. ידו בּעחת, literally, with the one (namely) of his hands that was doing the work. The suffix of ידו points to the genitive following. ואחת אחת, the one and the other hand. השּׁלח, not a missile, but a weapon that was stretched out, held forth, usually a sword or some defensive weapon: see rem. on <reference osisRef="Josh.2.8">Jos 2:8</reference>; 2Ch 32:5. The builders, on the contrary, needed both hands for their work: hence they had swords girt to their sides. “And he that sounded the trumpet was beside me.” Nehemiah, as superintendent of the work, stood at the head of his servants, ready to ward off any attack; hence the trumpeter was beside him, to be able to give to those employed on the wall the signal for speedy muster in case danger should threaten.
entries.b0c371f49a181c3ffeee18c424c99b5706692784: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.19-Neh.4.21">Neh 4:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen6547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6548" type="x-p"/> Hence he said to the nobles, the rulers, and the rest of the people, i.e., all employed in building, “The work is much (great) and wide, and we are separated upon the wall one far from another; in what place ye hear the sound of the trumpet, assemble yourselves to me: our God will fight for us.” - In <reference osisRef="Neh.4.15">Neh 4:15</reference> the whole is summed up, and for this purpose the matter of <reference osisRef="Neh.4.10">Neh 4:10</reference> is briefly repeated, to unite with it the further statement that they so laboured from early morning till late in the evening. “We (Nehemiah and his servants) laboured in the work, and half of them (of the servants) held the spears from the grey of dawn till the stars appeared.”
entries.00269a49545b56bf671d2bc728507b062f093d78: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.22">Neh 4:22</reference> <div eID="gen6548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6549" type="x-p"/> He took moreover, a further precaution: he said to the people (i.e., to the labourers on the wall, and not merely to the warriors of the community, as Bertheau supposes): Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, i.e., to remain together during the night also, and not be scattered through the surrounding district, “that they may be guardianship for us by night and labour by day.” The abstracts, guardianship and labour, stand for the concretes, guards and labourers. As לנוּ, <hi type="italic">to us</hi>, refers to the whole community separated on the walls, so is ונערו אישׁ to be understood of all the workers, and not of the fighting men only. From ונערו אישׁ it only appears that the fathers of families and master builders had servants with them as labourers.
entries.c42ea0c04b1091857c64a19eacb1077b3c17ffa3: <reference osisRef="Neh.4.23">Neh 4:23</reference> <div eID="gen6549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6550" type="x-p"/> Nehemiah, moreover, and his brethren (his kinsmen and the members of his house), and his servants, and the men of the guard in his retinue, were constantly in their clothes (“not putting off our clothes” to rest). The last words, המּים שׁלחו אישׁ are very obscure, and give no tolerable sense, whether we explain המּים of water for drinking or washing. Luther translates, Every one left off washing; but the words, Every one’s weapon was water, can never bear this sense. Roediger, in Gesen. <hi type="italic">Thes. s.v.</hi> שׁלח, seeks to alter המים into בידו, to which Böttcher (<hi type="italic">N. krit. Aehrenl</hi>. iii. p. 219) rightly objects: “how could בידו have been altered into המּים, or המּים have got into the text at all, if some portion of it had not been originally there? What this בידו expresses, would be far more definitely given with the very slight correction of changing the closing ם of המּים, and reading המינו = המינוּ (comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.19">2Sa 14:19</reference>); thus each had taken his missile on the right (in his right hand), naturally that he might be ready to discharge it in case of a hostile attack.” This conjecture seems to us a happy emendation of the unmeaning text, since נוּ might easily have been changed into ם; and we only differ in this matter from Böttcher, by taking שׁלח in its only legitimate meaning of weapon, and translating the words: And each laid his weapon on the right, viz., when he laid himself down at night to rest in his clothes, to be ready for fighting at the first signal from the watch.  <chapter eID="Neh.4"/> <div eID="gen6550" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 BUt it came to pass, that when <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 2. 10.</ns0:note> Sanballat heard that we built the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Pretending contempt in his words when he had grief in his Heart.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And he spake before his brethren <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Tobiah, v.</ns0:hi> 3. and <ns0:hi>Geshem, ch.</ns0:hi> 2. 19. and others, whom he calls <ns0:hi>his brethren,</ns0:hi> because of their conjunction with him in office and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terest.</ns0:note> and the army of Samaria <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Whom he designed hereby to incense against them, or at least to understand their minds herein.</ns0:note>, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>leave to themselves.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> fortifie themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Do they intend to begin, and finish the work, and keep the feast of dedication by sacrifice all in one day? for if they spend any long time about it, they cannot think that we and the rest of their Neighbours will suffer them to do it. Thus he persuaded himself and his compani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons, that their attempt was ridiculous; and this mistake kept him from giving them any disturbance, till it was too late. So God in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faruated him to his own grief and shame, and to the advantage of his people.</ns0:note>? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Will they pick up their broken stones out of the ruines, and patch them together, for other materials they want.</ns0:note> which are burnt <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Which stones were burnt, and broken, or consumed to pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der, to wit, by the Chaldeans when they took the City. See on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 3.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:370" />3 Now Tobiah the Ammonite <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> by him, and he said, even that which they build, if a fox go up <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He mentions the Foxes, because they were very numerous in those parts and because in the late desolations the Foxes did walk in the Mount, and City of <ns0:hi>Zion, Lamen.</ns0:hi> 5. 18. wherewith he seems to upbraid them.</ns0:note>, he shall even break down their stone-wall <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">It is so low, that a Fox can easily get to the top of it, and so weak, and done so hastily and carelesly, that the least thrust will tumble it down.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Hear, O our God, for we are <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>despite.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> despised: and turn their reproach upon their own head <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Let them be really as contemptible as they represent us to be. This and the following requests may seem harsh, but they were both just, as being directed against such malicious, inveterate, and implacable enemies to God, and to his People, and necessary for the vindication, and defence of Gods Honour, and Worship, and People.</ns0:note>, and give them for a prey in the land of captivity <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">let them be removed from our Neighbourhood, and carried into Captivity; and there let them find no favour, but fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther severity. Or, <ns0:hi>give them for a prey</ns0:hi> to their enemies, and let these carry them <ns0:hi>into the land of captivity.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 109. 14. 15.</ns0:note> cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Let their wickedness be in thy sight, so as to bring down deser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved judgments upon them, that either they may be convinced and reformed, or others may be warned by their example. God is said to cover or hide sin when he forbears to punish it.</ns0:note>; for they have provoked thee to anger before the builders <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> They have not only provoked us builders, but thee also. Or, <ns0:hi>they have provoked</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>derided the builders to their face. i. e.</ns0:hi> openly and impu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dently, in contempt of God, and of this work which is done by his direction and encouragement.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 So built we the wall: and all the wall was joyned together unto the half thereof <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either, 1. in length, or rather, 2. in heighth: for the whole circumference of the wall was distributed among the builders, who also had carried on the work, beginning at the sheep-gate, and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding there also, as appears from <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 1, 32. and <ns0:hi>the walls of Ierusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem</ns0:hi> are said to be <ns0:hi>made up,</ns0:hi> here v. 7.</ns0:note>: for the people had a mind to work.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 But it came to pass <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> when Sanballat, and To<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />biah, and the Arabians, and the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites, heard that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>healing went up to the wall.</ns0:hi> 2 Chr. 24. 13.</ns0:note> the walls of Jerusalem were made up, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> that the breaches began to be stopped <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That the breaches which the Chaldeans had made, and left in the walls, were well-nigh stopped up.</ns0:note>, then they were very wroth,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And conspired all of them together, to come <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> to fight against Jerusalem, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to make an error to it.</ns0:note> to hinder it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Nevertheless, we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night, because of them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And Judah <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Jews now dwelling in <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> to wit, some of them being partly terrified by their enemies, and partly wearied with hard and continual labours.</ns0:note> said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> much rubbish <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">More than we are able suddenly to remove.</ns0:note>, so that we are not able to build the wall <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Being forced to spend our time in removing the rub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bish, and other works imposed upon us; and therefore we must desist, at least for a season.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> They will invade you every way, by which we can come to you, or you to us; and therefore do you keep watch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es on every side. But these words may be otherwise rendred thus, <ns0:hi>On all parts where you shall be quiet, or at rest. (i. e.</ns0:hi> secure: for the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>Sc<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>ub</ns0:hi> signifies not only <ns0:hi>to return,</ns0:hi> but also <ns0:hi>to be quiet,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>at ease,</ns0:hi> as Hebricians know: they will be <ns0:hi>upon us, i. e.</ns0:hi> upon our peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and city <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> where you are. And they rather say <ns0:hi>upon us</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>upon you,</ns0:hi> to manifest their affection to them, and conjunction with them, and that they looked upon themselves as Members of the same Body and Church with them, and took what was design<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed or done against them, as if it were against themselves, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore gave them this friendly notice. Or the place may be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>They told this</ns0:hi> (to wit, the enemies intentions) <ns0:hi>to us ten times,</ns0:hi> coming <ns0:hi>from all places where they dwelt</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>rested</ns0:hi> (Heb. <ns0:hi>you rested.</ns0:hi> The second person being put for the third, as it is both in the Hebrew language, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 10. 19. 30. & 25. 18. and in the Hebrew Text, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22. 9. and in other languages and authors: of which, see my Latine <ns0:hi>Synopsis</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 10. 19. and that it is so here, we have the consent of the <ns0:hi>Seventy,</ns0:hi> and Arabick, and of some modern, and accurate Interpreters, who render it by a verb of the third person) <ns0:hi>about us;</ns0:hi> whence they came purposely to inform and warn us. Or thus, <ns0:hi>They told this to us ten times from all places whence they did re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turn to us.</ns0:hi> Which phrase of <ns0:hi>returning to us, i. e.</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> suits very well with those persons who came up with their brethren from <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and went thence into several parts of the country to dwell where they thought meet, and returned now, and at other times as they had occasion, to their brethren at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>

                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the LORD <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And it came to pass when our enemies heard that it was known unto us, and God had brought their counsel to nought, that we returned all of us to the wall, every one unto his work <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Our enemies being frustrated in their hopes, which were wholly built upon the secrecy, and suddenness of their attempt, we knowing this, returned to our business.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="17">17 They which built on the wall, and they that bare burdens, <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> those that laded, <ns0:hi>every one</ns0:hi> with one of his hands wrought in the work, and <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> the other <ns0:hi>hand</ns0:hi> held a weapon <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is not to be taken properly, for they could never have done their work with one hand, and the next verse tells us the sword was not in their hands, but by their sides; but figuratively; this being a proverbial speech, such as is frequent amongst the La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tines, as when they say of a man pretending kindness with evil de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign, <ns0:hi>He carries bread in one hand, and a stone in another.</ns0:hi>
